headline: Bulgaria elects its first woman president

sources.title: Initial results suggest Yotova wins runoff to become Bulgaria's first elected female president (AP)

Bulgaria's incumbent president Iotova wins runoff vote (RTE)
Iotova/Valchev Win with 58.16% of Votes with 72.65% of Tally Sheets Processed (BTA)

chunks.text: On November 1, 2026, Bulgarians {{voted in}} a woman as president for the first time. Bulgaria is a country in southeast Europe. The winner, Iliana Yotova, was already doing the job. As vice president, she {{took over}} as [[acting president]] in January 2026. Her [[longtime ally]], the elected president, had {{stepped down}} to run for parliament. His party won, and he became prime minister.

verbs.correct: To choose a leader by voting
verbs.wrong: To count ballots after an election
verbs.why: Many towns vote in a new mayor every four years. Our club votes in a new president each spring. On November 1, 2026, Bulgarians voted in a woman as president for the first time.

verbs.correct: To start a job after another person
verbs.wrong: To share a job with another person
verbs.why: A new coach takes over when the old one retires. My brother takes over at the store when my father goes home. Yotova took over as acting president in January 2026, when the elected president left.

verbs.wrong: To visit towns and meet voters
verbs.why: Many company leaders step down when they turn 65. A team captain sometimes steps down after a bad season. The elected president stepped down to run for parliament.

chunks.text: The vote was a [[runoff]], a second vote between the top two candidates. Yotova's [[rival]] was a former [[caretaker]] prime minister, a temporary leader before an election. [[Opposition parties]] {{lined up behind}} him. In the [[first round]] on October 25, Yotova won 35 percent to his 32. [[Turnout]], the share of people who vote, was a [[record low]] 23 percent. Most Bulgarians {{sat out}} that round. More {{turned out}} for the runoff, about 28 percent by early estimates.

verbs.correct: To support a person as a group
verbs.wrong: To pay a person to run a campaign
verbs.why: Party members often line up behind one candidate before an election. Workers line up behind a leader they trust. Opposition parties lined up behind Yotova's rival in the runoff.

verbs.correct: To choose not to take part
verbs.wrong: To wait in line at a voting place
verbs.why: Many people sit out local elections. Hurt players sit out the big game. Most Bulgarians sat out the first round of the election on October 25.

verbs.correct: To attend an event or vote
verbs.wrong: To change a vote at the last minute
verbs.why: Thousands of fans turn out for the town parade. Few people turn out for small local elections. More Bulgarians turned out for the runoff than for the first round.

chunks.text: Russia and the Ukraine war were major issues. In October, drones hit [[commercial ships]] off Bulgaria's coast and left 21 people missing. Both candidates {{spoke out}} against the attacks. The prime minister said the attacks seemed to help Russia, but his government says no [[evidence]] directly links them to Russia. In a debate, the rival {{called Yotova out}} for not blaming Russia directly. Yotova opposes [[military aid]] to Ukraine and says peace there can come only through [[negotiations]]. She supports Bulgaria's EU and NATO membership.

verbs.correct: To say publicly that you oppose something
verbs.wrong: To answer questions on a TV show
verbs.why: Students often speak out against unfair rules. Some workers speak out when a company breaks the law. Both candidates spoke out against the drone attacks on ships.

verbs.correct: To say publicly that someone did wrong
verbs.wrong: To ask someone to join a campaign
verbs.why: Good reporters call out leaders who lie. Fans often call out players who cheat. In a debate, the rival called Yotova out for not blaming Russia directly.

chunks.text: In the runoff, Yotova {{pulled ahead}}. With most [[ballots]] counted, she had about 58 percent to his 39. Bulgaria's president has [[limited powers]] and does not run the government. Parliament must {{sign off on}} all major policies. The president leads the [[armed forces]] and can [[veto]], or {{turn down}}, new laws. Yotova's win lets the prime minister's allies {{hold on to}} the presidency. [[Observers]] warn that one party may hold too much power.

verbs.wrong: To win by only a few votes
verbs.why: The faster runner often pulls ahead in the last mile. Our team usually pulls ahead in the second half. Yotova pulled ahead of her rival in the runoff and won about 58 percent.

verbs.wrong: To write the first draft of a plan
verbs.why: A manager signs off on every large payment. The city council signs off on new building plans. In Bulgaria, parliament must sign off on all major policies.
Banks turn down many loan requests. Good colleges turn down a lot of students. Bulgaria's president can veto, or turn down, new laws.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To give a job to a close friend
verbs.why: Most leaders try to hold on to power. Some teams hold on to their best players for years. Yotova's win lets the prime minister's allies hold on to the presidency.

wordDefs.def: A person who does the president's job for a time without being elected
ex: The college named an acting president while it searched for a new leader.

wordDefs.def: A person who has supported you and worked with you for many years
ex: The mayor gave the job to a longtime ally.
Her longtime ally on the city council moved to another state.
He lost a longtime ally when his partner retired.

wordDefs.def: A second vote between the top candidates when no one won the first vote
ex: The two top candidates for mayor will meet in a runoff.
Our state holds a runoff if no one gets half the votes.
She won the runoff by just 200 votes.

wordDefs.def: A person who competes against you for the same thing
ex: The senator shook hands with her rival after the debate.
His main rival for the job has more experience.
She beat her rival in the final race.

wordDefs.def: Holding a government job only for a short time until an election
ex: The caretaker government can't start big new programs.
A retired judge became caretaker leader of the country.

wordDefs.def: Political groups that are not part of the government
ex: Opposition parties voted against the budget.

wordDefs.def: The first of two or more votes or stages in a contest
ex: Our team lost in the first round of the tournament.

wordDefs.def: The number or share of people who take part in an event or vote
ex: Rain kept turnout low at the street fair.

The organizers were happy with the turnout at the concert.
Home sales fell to a record low in March.
The lake dropped to a record low during the dry summer.
Unemployment in the state reached a record low.

wordDefs.def: Large boats used for business, such as moving goods
ex: Most of the world's goods travel on commercial ships.
The new port can handle very large commercial ships.
All commercial ships must follow strict safety rules.

wordDefs.def: Facts or signs that show something is true
ex: The police found new evidence in the case.

Do you have any evidence for that claim?

wordDefs.def: Formal talks to reach an agreement
ex: The negotiations between the union and the company lasted a month.
After long negotiations, they agreed on a price.

wordDefs.def: Weapons, money or training that one country gives another for its defense
ex: Congress voted on a new military aid bill.

wordDefs.def: Papers that people mark to show their vote
ex: Workers counted the ballots late into the night.

wordDefs.def: Only a small amount of official control
ex: The city board has limited powers over schools.
Under the rules, the club president has limited powers.

wordDefs.def: A country's army, navy and air force
ex: Her brother joined the armed forces after high school.
The country's armed forces helped after the flood.
Many people in the armed forces live far from home.

wordDefs.def: To officially refuse to approve a new law
ex: The governor may veto the new tax bill.

Can the mayor veto a decision by the city council?

wordDefs.def: People who watch events closely and comment on them
ex: Many observers expected a close game.
Some observers think prices will rise again.
Foreign observers watched the vote in several cities.

mainIdea.s: A woman has won Bulgaria's presidency in an election for the first time, after a second vote. The winner already held the job for months as acting leader, and the post has limited powers.
mainIdea.why: Bulgarians voted in Yotova in the runoff. She took over as acting president in January, and parliament must sign off on all major policies.

mainIdea.s: Bulgarians have chosen a female leader with a large lead, ending months of rule by a temporary cabinet. She will now run national policy herself, and lawmakers will play only a small part.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Bulgaria's president does not run the government. Parliament must sign off on all major policies, and the prime minister's allies hold on to power.

mainIdea.s: Bulgaria has agreed to send more weapons to Ukraine following drone strikes near its coast. Lawmakers approved the plan in November, and the first shipments should leave by next spring.
mainIdea.why: The news here is the runoff, in which Yotova pulled ahead and won. She opposes military aid to Ukraine, and no such plan was approved.

tf.s: Bulgarians voted in a woman as president for the first time.
tf.why: Bulgarians voted in Yotova in the runoff on November 1, 2026. No woman had been elected to the job before.

tf.s: Yotova took over as acting president after she won the runoff.
tf.why: She took over as acting president in January 2026, months before the runoff.

tf.s: Most Bulgarians turned out to vote in the first round.
tf.why: Most Bulgarians sat out the first round. Turnout was a record low 23 percent.

tf.s: Both candidates spoke out against the drone attacks on ships.
tf.why: Both spoke out against the attacks, which hit commercial ships off the coast of Bulgaria.

tf.s: Yotova's rival called her out for not blaming Russia directly.
tf.why: He called her out in a debate. She said peace can come only through negotiations.

tf.s: Bulgaria's president can make major policies without parliament.
tf.why: The president has limited powers. Parliament must sign off on all major policies.

lines.text: Did you see the news from Bulgaria? Bulgarians {{voted in}} their first woman president.
Her name is Iliana Yotova. She {{took over}} as acting president in January.
Wait, so she already had the job? How did that happen?
The elected president {{stepped down}} to run for parliament. Now he's prime minister.
At first, yes. The first round was [[a tight race]], 35 to 32 percent.
A banker who led the government for a short time. Opposition parties {{lined up behind}} him.
Did a lot of people vote?
Turnout was low. Most people {{sat out}} the first round, and not many more {{turned out}} for the second.
Some voters didn't like either candidate. One man said he just picked [[the lesser of two evils]].
So who won in the end?
Yotova {{pulled ahead}} and won [[by a wide margin]], about 58 percent to 39.
Does she have much power now?
Not a lot. Parliament has to {{sign off on}} all major policies, though she can {{turn down}} new laws.
[[You have to admit]], she's the first woman elected to that job. Well, [[there's a first time for everything]].

expressions.def: A contest in which the two sides are almost equal
ex: It's a tight race for governor.
The final was a tight race until the last lap.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is true, even if you don't like it
ex: You have to admit, the new bus is faster.

expressions.def: The less bad choice when both choices are bad
ex: Both plans cost money, so we chose the lesser of two evils.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone won with a much higher score or total
ex: Our team won by a wide margin.
She beat the other candidates by a wide margin.

expressions.expr: there's a first time for everything
expressions.def: Used to say that even a new or surprising thing has to happen once
ex: I've never cooked for ten people, but there's a first time for everything.
My grandfather just sent his first text. There's a first time for everything.
